samples.text:
Today children usually have much more toys, clothes and electronic devices than children in the past. This essay will explain why this happen and how it affects their development.

There are several reasons for this change. Firstly, many families today are richer than before, so parents can afford to buy more things for their children. Secondly, most families have only one or two children, so parents and grandparents spend all their money on them. Also, toys are cheaper now because factories produce them in large numbers. Another reason is advertising. Children see adverts on television and YouTube and they ask their parents to buy the new toy. Some parents who work long hours also buy presents because they feel guilty that they do not spend enough time with their kids.

In my opinion, having too many possessions has more negative effects than positive effects on children. Children who get everything they want may not learn the value of money and they can become spoiled. For example, when a child has twenty toys, he often gets bored quickly and do not take care of them. Moreover, they have less chance to use their imagination, because in the past children made games with simple things like sticks and boxes. However, some toys, for example puzzles or building blocks, can help children to develop their skills and creativity.

In conclusion, children have more possessions today because families are richer, toys are cheap and advertising is powerful. Although some toys are educational, I believe that too many things can make children spoiled and less creative, so parents should buy less toys for them.

samples.text:
Compared with previous generations, many children today grow up surrounded by a large number of toys, gadgets and other possessions. This essay will examine the main causes of this change and argue that, although some possessions can be beneficial, having too many can hinder a child's development.

The most obvious explanation is rising prosperity. In many countries, households have more disposable income than they did several decades ago, and mass production has made toys and clothing far cheaper. At the same time, families have become smaller, so the attention and spending of parents, grandparents and other relatives are concentrated on fewer children. Commercial pressure also plays a major part. Children are exposed to constant advertising through television, online videos and games, and toy companies regularly release new versions of popular products, which creates a desire to keep up with friends. In addition, busy working parents sometimes use gifts to compensate for limited time spent together.

The effects of this abundance on development are mixed but mostly negative. On the positive side, educational toys, books and construction sets can stimulate curiosity and help children develop problem-solving and motor skills. However, when children have too many possessions, they tend to value each one less and may move quickly from one toy to other without engaging deeply with any of them. Many educators believe that a certain amount of boredom encourages creativity, and a child with only a few simple items is more likely to invent games and stories. Furthermore, receiving new things frequently may lead children to associate happiness with ownership, which can make it harder for them to learn patience and gratitude.

In conclusion, children own more than ever because families are wealthier, goods are cheaper and marketing is more intense. While carefully chosen toys can support learning, an excess of possessions can reduce creativity and encourage materialistic attitudes.
samples.why: Clear position with both questions addressed and developed · balanced discussion of effects · good cohesion and paragraphing · appropriate less common vocabulary (disposable income, hinder) · largely accurate with one minor slip.

samples.text:
A glance into many modern children's bedrooms reveals shelves crowded with toys, games and electronic devices on a scale that would have astonished earlier generations. This abundance is largely a product of economic and social change, and while it is not wholly harmful, I believe it often works against the qualities that children most need to develop.

Several forces lie behind this shift. Greater affluence and the global manufacturing of inexpensive goods mean that toys which were once special treats are now everyday purchases. Demographic change has amplified the effect: with fewer children per family, and often several grandparents eager to give presents, gifts that were once shared among siblings are now lavished on one or two children. Marketing, meanwhile, has become more direct and persistent. Children encounter advertising through online videos and games as well as television, and the constant release of new models and collectable ranges fuels a sense that what they have is never quite enough. Some parents, pressed for time, may also use gifts as a substitute for attention.

The developmental consequences depend partly on what children own, but quantity matters. Well-chosen toys such as building sets, art materials and books can foster creativity, concentration and fine motor skills. Yet when possessions are plentiful, each one tends to be valued less, and children may flit between them without the sustained engagement that deep play requires. A child with a cardboard box and a few figures is often forced to invent entire worlds, whereas one surrounded by ready-made entertainment has less need for imagination. There is also a risk that a steady stream of new items teaches children to seek satisfaction through acquisition, making patience, gratitude and the ability to cope with disappointment harder to learn.

In conclusion, children own more because of rising wealth, smaller families and relentless marketing. Although some possessions can enrich development, an excess tends to weaken imagination and encourage materialistic habits, so fewer, better-chosen items are generally preferable.
samples.why: Both questions answered in depth with a clear, qualified position · well-sequenced, fully supported ideas · wide, precise vocabulary (affluence, lavished, flit between) · wide range of accurate structures.
